clue.text: Given early nourishment by an apostle, perhaps

definitions.text: Given early nourishment by an apostle, perhaps

parts.words: Given early nourishment by an apostle, perhaps
parts.note: an apostle spoon is a traditional christening spoon topped with a figure of an apostle, so a baby fed from one is literally nourished by it

explanation.surface: A biblical image of an infant being fed by one of the disciples.
explanation.walkthrough: Apostle spoons, with a saint's figure on the handle, were a traditional British christening present; the clue reads the apostle as that spoon.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means having been fed with a spoon as a baby, and figuratively being given everything without effort.

clue.text: Picture taken outside airport showing sort of rock

indicators.note: the picture's letters are placed around the airport's name, enclosing it

parts.note: PIC is a short form of picture
Luton is an airport serving London

explanation.surface: A photograph of some rock formation shot outside an airport.
explanation.walkthrough: LUTON is an airport north of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Plutonic rocks are igneous rocks formed deep underground, like granite.

clue.text: Desperate hunt on to capture royal fugitive

indicators.note: the scrambled letters close around the royal abbreviation, taking it prisoner
desperate suggests wild disorder, so the letters of the words are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the royal cipher of the Queen

explanation.surface: A frantic manhunt to catch a royal who has escaped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desperate' scrambles 'hunt on' and 'to capture' wraps it around the royal cipher; 'hunt' tempts as part of the definition, but the fugitive is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the run is fleeing capture, an escapee.

clue.text: Skirt ornamentation needing warm covering underneath

parts.note: fur is an animal's warm coat
below means underneath

explanation.surface: A frill on a skirt that needs a warm lining beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: A furbelow is a flounce or frill on a skirt or petticoat.

clue.text: Potter getting involved with tradesmen in large shop

indicators.note: the two words become entangled with each other, mixing their letters into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A potter mixing with tradesmen inside a big store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting involved' mixes POTTER and TRADESMEN together; 'with' only joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: A department store is a big retail outlet selling many kinds of goods in separate sections.

clue.text: Chaff ordered to keep one horse

indicators.note: the word for ordered holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: bade is the past tense of bid, ordered
I is the Roman numeral for one
a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: Feed that someone has been told to set aside for a single horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chaff' looks like horse feed, fitting the surface, but here it is the verb-noun for teasing talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaff as a noun is light-hearted teasing, the same as playful banter.

clue.text: Bliss when one's featured in review

indicators.note: the piece for one's appears within the word for review

parts.note: a parade is a military review of troops
one's read as one is gives I + S

explanation.surface: Delight at being mentioned in a critic's review.
explanation.walkthrough: 'review' is not a critique but a military inspection, a PARADE.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise is a state of perfect happiness, heaven on earth.

clue.text: Always accepted in payment with deep respect

indicators.note: the word for always is taken into the word for payment

parts.note: rent is a regular payment for property
ever means always

explanation.surface: A payment that is always received with great deference.
explanation.definitionFit: Reverent describes an attitude of awe and veneration.

clue.text: Daring behaviour, inserting plug in leak

indicators.note: the plug's letters are put into the leak's letters

parts.note: an escape of gas or water is a leak
a plug is a promotion, an advertisement, AD

explanation.surface: A bold act of stopping up a leak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plug' suggests a bung, but it is the publicity sense, an AD; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapade is a reckless adventure or prank.

clue.text: Flatter book, say, used at university

parts.note: utter means say
up means in residence at university, as in up at Oxford

explanation.surface: Praise a book that is used at college.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a student is 'up' at university while in residence. 'used' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To butter someone up is to win them over with excessive compliments.

clue.text: Police coming round in a rage — give up!

indicators.note: the turned police letters sit inside the word for rage

parts.note: bate is an old word for a fit of temper

indicators.note: coming round means the police letters turn back to front

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of the British police

explanation.surface: Police arriving in a fury tell someone to surrender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming round' turns the police abbreviation backwards; the rage word is a dated British term for a fit of temper, rarely seen outside crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: To abdicate is to renounce a throne or responsibility, to relinquish it.

clue.text: One further back on line given warning at Paddington, perhaps

parts.note: fore is the golfer's shouted warning
Paddington is the famous fictional bear from Peru

explanation.surface: A traveller further down the platform warned at Paddington station.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddington is a London station, fitting the 'line' of the surface, but here it is the children's-book bear. The 'line' is a family line of descent.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancestor stands earlier in a family's line of descent.

clue.text: Negotiate one's fee, finally, for formal work

parts.note: to treat is to negotiate terms
one's read as one is gives I + S

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word fee

explanation.surface: A consultant bargaining over their fee for some formal job.
explanation.definitionFit: A treatise is a formal written study of a subject.

clue.text: Appreciation of college rhyme chaps used in performance

indicators.note: the other pieces are placed inside the word for performance

parts.note: an act is a performance
a word that rhymes with college, as in the Oxford verse 'what I don't know isn't knowledge'
men are chaps

explanation.surface: Thanks for a bit of college verse recited by men in a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'college rhyme' asks for a word rhyming with college, a famous pairing in an old Oxford verse about Benjamin Jowett.
explanation.definitionFit: Acknowledgement is recognition or gratitude shown for something.

clue.text: Drunk in a bar, so producing superficial damage

indicators.note: drunk suggests staggering disorder, so the letters reel into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone drunk in a pub picks up a scrape or two.
explanation.definitionFit: An abrasion is a graze, where skin is scraped off the surface.

clue.text: Recoil from bribe

definitions.meaning: the backward jolt of a gun when fired
an illicit payment made in return for a favour

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a gun's backward jerk and an illegal payback to secure business.

clue.text: Cook I reprove — such fruit's too old

indicators.note: to cook is to fiddle or doctor, so the letters are tampered with and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A chef being told off over fruit that has gone past its best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'such fruit's' tells you the definition 'too old' is about fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit past its best has gone soft and squashy through age.

clue.text: Gallons required to get a feeble illumination from fuel

parts.note: slight means feeble or flimsy

explanation.surface: Gallons of fuel needed just to produce a dim light.
explanation.definitionFit: Gas lighting, burning coal gas, was the old way of lighting streets and homes.

clue.text: Strict disciplinarian time after time interrupting soldier

indicators.note: after places the first time at the end, following the rest
the second time breaks into the soldier word

parts.note: a marine is a soldier serving at sea

explanation.surface: A sergeant who keeps cutting into a soldier's routine over and over.
explanation.definitionFit: A martinet is a stickler for rules, a rigid enforcer of discipline.

clue.text: Mean-spirited team left on coach, say

parts.note: near is an old word for stingy or mean
a side is a team

explanation.surface: A stingy team left behind on a coach trip.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the nearside of a vehicle is its left, the side nearest the kerb.
explanation.definitionFit: The nearside is the kerb side of a vehicle, which on British roads is the left.

clue.text: Withdraw soldiers hemmed in, lacking courage

indicators.note: the soldiers are surrounded by the letters of the word for withdraw

parts.note: to recant is to withdraw a statement
RE, the Royal Engineers, are British army soldiers

explanation.surface: Soldiers pulling back when trapped, having lost their nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: Recreant is an archaic word for cowardly or craven.

clue.text: Advantageous payment covering organised workers in retirement

indicators.note: the payment word wraps around the workers' letters

parts.note: a salary is a regular payment

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: TU, a trade union, is a body of organised workers

explanation.surface: A pension covering unionised staff once they retire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retirement' tempts you toward a pension, but it only signals reading the workers' abbreviation backwards before the salary wraps it.
explanation.definitionFit: Salutary means beneficial, having a good effect.

clue.text: A couple of transporters turned round at front of tarmac to take off

indicators.note: each of the two transport words is written back to front where it stands

parts.note: a bus is one transporter
a cart is another transporter

indicators.note: front of picks out the opening letter of the word tarmac

explanation.surface: Two aircraft turning round on the apron before departure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned round' turns each vehicle in place. 'take off' suggests a plane departing; here it means deduct.
explanation.definitionFit: To subtract is to deduct, removing one quantity from another.

clue.text: Material publication has to decline

parts.note: an organ is a newspaper or journal of a party or group
to die is to decline or fade away

explanation.surface: Copy from a periodical that is going downhill.
explanation.definitionFit: Organdie is a fine, stiff, translucent cotton fabric.

clue.text: Happen to find bird nesting as resident

indicators.note: the bird settles inside the word for happen

parts.note: to occur is to happen
pie is an old name for the magpie

explanation.surface: Coming across a bird living in a nest.
explanation.walkthrough: PIE is an old name for the magpie, used in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: An occupier is someone who lives in or holds a property.

clue.text: Having the right finish to keep in style

indicators.note: the finish word holds the style word within it

parts.note: end means finish
a title is a style or form of address

explanation.surface: A finishing school entitled to keep someone stylish.
explanation.definitionFit: Being entitled means being qualified or allowed to do or claim something.
